implementation_notes: Functions are first-class objects that can be passed, returned and assigned (MDN), so composition is ordinary code: `const pipe = (...steps) => x => steps.reduce((acc, step) => step(acc), x)` or an inline `x => g(f(x))`. JavaScript has no standard-library compose - the TC39 Function.pipe/flow proposal is still a proposal - so the classic helper is re-created per project, and library equivalents (Ramda's pipe, lodash/fp's flow, fp-ts's flow) are the alternative for teams already writing data-last curried code. Inline arrows stay the default for a single use; the helper earns its place when the chain is stored, passed or built from data.
pitfalls: Passing a method into a chain detaches it from its receiver: extract a wrapper (`x => obj.method(x)`) or bind it, otherwise `this` is undefined at call time.
A promise-returning step silently poisons a synchronous chain - every later step then receives a Promise; use a promise-aware pipe or explicit awaits.

pipe and flow mean different directions in different libraries (Ramda pipe is left-to-right, lodash flow is left-to-right while flowRight is not), so a chain copied between codebases can run in reverse.
